single_story.note: All sources cover the same Altman/Politico Decoded interview and its context. Core quotes are from Politico, which I did not open directly; I read it via Fortune, Fox News (citing Reuters), TNW and Storyboard18.

the_news.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico's new Decoded newsletter, published around Oct. 5, 2026, that the world should accept some bad things happening for AI's benefits, and he said OpenAI and Anthropic differ sharply on AI rules.

why_it_matters.text: The remarks show a public split between OpenAI (broad access, lighter-touch regulation) and Anthropic (more cautious pacing of frontier AI) while the Trump administration sets up a federal AI task force.

Fortune says the tone is a shift from Altman's recent, more cautious Fortune interview, in which he called a 10% risk of AI killing us all by the end of the decade unacceptable and said no lab has solved alignment.

facts.text: Altman gave the interview to Politico for the first edition of Decoded, a new daily tech newsletter and podcast that launches Monday (Oct. 5, 2026).
notes: TNW says it has not seen the full interview. All coverage I read is second-hand from Politico.

facts.text: Altman said he would not trade the benefits of AI for a guarantee of no major hacks, misuse or scams, because he believes people will do far more good than bad with it.
notes: This is Altman's own view, not an independently verified finding.

facts.text: Altman said some people think AI is so dangerous that a single lab should hold it and dole out the benefits. He said he understands that view but disagrees, and he called it a 'completely unacceptable trade-off'.
notes: Storyboard18 (citing Reuters) frames this as describing a model where one lab controls access, which would limit people's agency.

facts.text: Altman said there is 'a lot of daylight' between OpenAI and Anthropic on AI governance, and OpenAI backs a 'lighter-touch regulatory approach'.
notes: 'Lot of daylight' appears only in Storyboard18. 'Lighter-touch regulatory approach' appears in Fox News (quoted) and is paraphrased by Storyboard18.

facts.text: Per TNW's paraphrase of Politico, Altman said the world should not accept the worst risks, such as a serious loss of control to AI.
notes: Single source, paraphrase only.

facts.text: Fortune says Altman was more cautious in a recent Fortune interview. There he said a 10% risk of AI killing us all by the end of the decade is unacceptable and that OpenAI has not taken and would not take that risk.
notes: This is a Fortune newsletter summary; I did not open the underlying interview.

facts.text: An Anthropic spokesperson told Politico that Anthropic's proposed rules apply only to frontier models, the most advanced AI systems.
facts.claim_by: Anthropic spokesperson, via TNW's account of Politico
notes: Single source.

facts.text: The comments came about three weeks after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay asking the industry to 'pace the frontier' (slow how fast AI models improve), which Altman backed the same day.
notes: Storyboard18 says Amodei called for this 'in September'. Storyboard18 says Altman's latest comments put greater emphasis on broad public access while accepting some risk.

facts.text: President Trump announced a 'Super Intelligence Force' on Sunday (Oct. 4) to coordinate federal engagement with AI. The White House says its task force has 120 days to examine AI risks and opportunities and is chaired by DNI Jay Clayton.
notes: The Wall Street Journal first reported the task-force details, per Fox News. Fortune says Trump declared it 'yesterday'. TNW describes Politico's coverage as touching on a Trump 'order to rename AI superintelligence', which differs from this framing.

facts.text: OpenAI is one of four AI companies due to testify under oath at a New York City Council hearing on AI safety on Monday (Oct. 5).
notes: Single source. Fox News separately reports a former Anthropic/OpenAI researcher, Jacob Coxon, testifying at that hearing.

facts.text: Separately, Altman posted on X over the weekend that he is 'very uncomfortable' with people ascribing religious force to AI models. The Independent reads this as an apparent shot at Anthropic, though he named no company.
notes: The Independent's reading is interpretation. It is a separate remark from the Politico interview.

background.text: Anthropic has increasingly highlighted AI risks. Its IPO prospectus warns of possible 'catastrophic or existential risks to humanity', and Reuters reported last month that it warned advanced models can sometimes act against their creators' intentions.
notes: Storyboard18 relays Reuters. I did not open Reuters.

background.text: The Trump administration has largely resisted new AI-specific restrictions, arguing that tighter regulation could undermine US competitiveness against China.
notes: Single source.

quotes.text: I wouldn't take a trade of saying, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen' … Because I think people will do tremendously—orders of magnitude more—good stuff than bad stuff.
quotes.speaker: Sam Altman
notes: Fortune uses an ellipsis between the two parts. Fox spells it 'tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff'.

quotes.text: I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'

Whether OpenAI or Anthropic gave any further public response is not covered.
